scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Akdağmadeni halay emerged in the early 20th century in the Akdağmadeni district of Yozgat Province in Central Anatolia.
It was developed by Pontic Greek miners who migrated to the area from the Eastern Black Sea region.
Known originally in Pontic Greek as Khalái (Χαλάι), the dance took its name from the refrain of a Turkish folk song popular among these Turkish-speaking Pontic Greek miners.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally performed by mining families as a social and community dance, it served as a shared cultural tradition among Pontic Greek and Anatolian communities in Yozgat.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a semi-circular or line formation with participants holding each other by the fingers, hands, or shoulders.
Dancers execute a slow-paced sequence characterized by intense bending movements and rhythmic foot strikes.
The sequence begins on the right foot, taking three steps diagonally to the right.
Watch for Left Foot Inward Placement.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Hamit Zübeyir Koşay and İshak Işıtman documented the broader halay tradition in their 1932 ethnographic compilation Anadilden Derlemeler.

Following its adoption in Akdağmadeni, variants of the dance spread to Sivas, Çorum, Kayseri, and other areas of northern Cappadocia, each establishing localized characteristics while preserving the basic footwork structure.

Akdağmadeni halay belongs to the broader halay family of Anatolian circular and line dances and shares structural similarities with regional Caucasian and Middle Eastern line traditions such as Azerbaijani Yalli.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Akdağmadeni halay is parent of Halay: Akdağmadeni halay (Khalái) provided the name and early model for the wider Turkish halay genre.
Akdağmadeni halay is sibling of Yallı: Shares line and circle floor patterns and similar instrumentation across Turkic/Anatolian traditions.
